headline: Trump said Iran could "take out" LA. California erupted.
summary: At a Nebraska rally on Monday, Trump called the Iran war's high gas prices "a small price to pay". Then: "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego." Governor Newsom called him "deranged and dangerous". The White House says he meant a nuclear Iran would have threatened both cities.

cover_question.q: Did the president actually mean that?

cover_answer: The White House says no. California heard it anyway.
table_question: Does "I didn't mean it that way" undo what you said?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president gave a speech about the war with Iran and said something that sounded like he would let a city in California get hurt. Lots of grown-ups got angry, and his team says he meant the opposite. It was words at a speech, like a loud wrong thing shouted at a game, and nothing happened to any city. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Shielded: a six-year-old can't do anything with a threat to a city. If it reaches them, nothing happened is the script.
5-7.why_long: Cantor's work on fright says a young child fears the vivid, physical threat, and a president saying a city could be taken out is that, so a parent does not raise it. If it arrives, the script gives one fact to hold: words at a speech, and nothing happened. Expect "is our town next?" No.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Gas prices are high because of the war with Iran. At a rally, Trump called that a small price to pay, then said Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego. California's leaders fired back. The White House says he meant a nuclear Iran was the threat. A replay: the words are on the record.
8-12.why: A chain they can follow: war, gas prices, a line at a rally, the backlash, the walk-back.
8-12.why_long: This age is testing whether adults keep their own rules, and the chain is one they can follow: a war, gas prices, a line at a rally, the backlash, the walk-back. The replay is the mechanism: the words are quoted, so they can judge them against the White House's version. Expect "which is it?" Both.

13-17.script: Did the president actually mean that? The quote: "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay." The White House says he meant a nuclear Iran was the threat. Does the walk-back settle it, or do the words stand?
13-17.why: Kuhn: argument is a practised skill. The quote and the walk-back, side by side.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the president said those words, and his office says he meant the opposite. Kuhn's point is that argument is a practised skill, so the script hands them the quote and the clarification side by side. Expect "would anyone else get away with that?"

5-7.q: Is Iran going to hurt Los Angeles?
5-7.a: No one attacked anything. It was words at a speech, and his team says he meant the opposite.

8-12.q: Why would he say that about his own country?
8-12.a: He was arguing the war is worth it. His office says Iran was the threat.
Both have big military bases. Their mayors say a president protects them.

13-17.q: Did the president actually mean that?
13-17.a: His office says no: he meant a nuclear Iran. The quote is on the record.

13-17.q: Why does a line at a rally matter so much?
13-17.a: San Diego's bases employ 136,000 people. Its mayor says it is "not expendable".
